105.bp: AI agents are starting to do real work on the web—opening links, filling forms, booking tickets—by calling external tools through a system called Model Context Protocol. The problem is that if someone poisons those tools or the data feeding them, the agent's reasoning can get corrupted mid-task, leading to wrong actions or security breaches. We need a way to catch and fix these corruptions automatically, not just detect them.
105.wh: Existing defenses stop at detection: they flag that something went wrong. But they don't fix it. When an agent has already made a bad decision because a tool gave it poisoned output, you can't just ignore it and move forward—the agent has already taken the wrong action. You need to backtrack, figure out what the root cause was, and have the agent re-think from that point. The challenge is doing this without constantly re-running everything (which would be slow).

When an agent has already made a bad decision because a tool gave it poisoned output, you can't just ignore it and move forward—the agent has already taken the wrong action. You need to backtrack, figure out what the root cause was, and have the agent re-think from that point. The challenge is doing this without constantly re-running everything (which would be slow).
105.ap: MCPFixGen saves checkpoints at high-risk moments (when the agent is about to call a tool). When something goes wrong, it rewinds to a checkpoint, identifies the bad tool output by looking at how hard the agent's brain was 'paying attention' to that tool call, then masks out that poisoned input and tells the agent to try again. This is like rewinding a movie to just before a character opens a bad letter, then having them skip that letter and continue.
105.ww: This works because poison usually shows up as a sudden shift in the agent's reasoning patterns. By tracking which tools the agent is paying attention to at each moment, you can spot when it suddenly trusts a tool that normally gets low attention. And by masking out just that one bad input instead of throwing away the whole sequence, the agent only has to re-compute from the poisoned point, not restart from scratch.
105.po: MCPFixGen lets AI agents automatically recover from tool poisoning attacks without human help, reducing both the time and cost of fixing mistakes. This makes browser-based autonomous agents safe enough for real deployment, where mistakes cost time or money.

106.bp: Companies make environmental claims ("we cut emissions by 50%", "our packaging is eco-friendly") to look good to investors and customers. But many of these claims are exaggerated, misleading, or just false—a practice called greenwashing. We need an automated way to fact-check these claims against real evidence, so regulators and buyers can trust sustainability reports.
106.wh: Checking a greenwashing claim manually is hard. You have to find the company's actual ESG (environmental, social, governance) reports, dig through dense tables of data, cross-reference industry benchmarks, and decide if what the company claims matches what it actually did. This takes human time and expertise. An AI that just reads the claim and guesses will hallucinate evidence. You need the AI to cite real documents.
106.ap: EmeraldApp gives the AI three ways to find evidence. The first digs through a database of ESG report chunks using semantic search (finding similar ideas, not just keyword matches). The second consults a hand-built knowledge graph of sustainability facts (like 'this company's solar capacity in 2024'). The third combines both. For each claim, the app either confirms it's real, flags it as greenwashing, or abstains if evidence is missing. It also logs every claim checked so auditors can review the history.
106.ww: By grounding the AI's answer in retrieved documents rather than letting it make up facts, you ensure the AI can point to real evidence. The combination of semantic search and structured knowledge facts covers both the messiness of real reports and the precision needed for factual claims. Logging everything adds accountability—companies can't deny what was checked.
106.po: EmeraldApp lets regulators, investors, and consumers verify sustainability claims instantly instead of waiting for audits. It flags probable greenwashing and shows the evidence, raising the cost of making false claims and making real sustainability data more visible and trustworthy.

107.bp: Someone shows you a photo and says 'I want something like this but with a red dress instead of blue.' You need to find similar photos in a database where the user's description has been applied—so the system understands both what the image shows and how language modifies it. This is harder than normal image search because you have to extract and change specific visual details based on natural-language instructions.
107.wh: The obvious approach—just search for 'red dress' in the image database—misses the nuance. The user is saying 'the composition and pose from this photo, but with different colors or items.' You have to extract the right parts of the reference image (what matters: pose, background, context; what doesn't: the blue dress color) and then use language to imagine what the dress should become. This means figuring out which visual features to keep and which to discard, which is different for every image and query.
107.ap: MCoT-MVS uses a large vision-language model to think through the problem step by step: 'What should I keep from this image? What should I remove? What's the new target?' Those answers guide two separate attention mechanisms that zoom in on different parts of the reference image—one picks out important small regions (patches), the other picks out complete objects (like 'the whole dress'). Then a fusion module combines what the system kept, what it imagined from the text, and the new target description into a single query that searches the database.
107.ww: Reasoning out loud (chain-of-thought) forces the model to decompose the problem instead of trying to solve it all at once. By using the reasoning output to guide visual attention, the system stops getting distracted by irrelevant details. And by separating fine-grained details (patches) from object-level choices (the full dress), the system can handle both small tweaks and large changes.
107.po: The system now finds better matching images when users describe 'same pose, different color' or 'same style, different size.' Experiments on two real datasets show it beats other methods, making composed image retrieval more useful for shopping, design inspiration, and content discovery.

108.bp: When child abuse material is reported online, specialists need to classify it quickly—partly to prioritize resources, but crucially to identify the age of the child, which has huge legal and investigative implications. Current methods rely on seeing faces clearly, but that's not always possible due to image quality, angle, or intentional obscuring. We need a way to estimate age even when the face is not visible.
108.wh: Face-based age estimation fails when the image shows only body shapes (silhouettes), which is common in abuse materials. But body proportions do correlate with age—children have different proportions than adults—and relative features matter (this person's head is smaller compared to their body, suggesting youth). However, there's natural variation: two 10-year-olds can have very different builds. You need a system that learns what proportions most strongly predict age groups and can compare individuals fairly.
108.ap: The researchers train neural networks on multiple related tasks at once: age estimation, gender prediction, height estimation—all from silhouettes. This multitask approach forces the network to learn general body-shape features that apply across related tasks. They also add a pairwise learning step: instead of just classifying one image as 'child' or 'adult,' the system compares pairs of people and learns 'person A is younger than person B.' This relative comparison is more robust than absolute guessing.
108.ww: Multitask learning works because all those tasks (age, gender, height) rely on overlapping body-shape patterns. Learning one task helps with the others. Pairwise comparison is more stable because it doesn't require the model to perfectly calibrate an absolute age estimate—it just needs to rank relative to other bodies, which is easier. Together, these reduce mistakes by 14–21%.
108.po: Experts can now classify suspected abuse materials more accurately even when faces are hidden, speeding up initial triage and improving the reliability of age determination for investigators. This helps law enforcement and platforms respond faster to reports.

109.bp: Mobile phones rely on SIM cards to prove you are who you say you are. But recently, hackers stole millions of SIM card records, exposing personal data and allowing impersonation. We need a way for you to prove your identity to the network without ever storing a secret on a SIM card that could be breached. Zero-knowledge proofs offer a way: prove you know a secret without revealing it.
109.wh: Traditional SIM authentication stores a key on the SIM card. If the card's data is stolen, the thief can pretend to be you. Moving the secret to the cloud makes it a juicy target for hackers—they break in once and compromise millions of users. You need a system where each person proves they have a valid key without anyone, including the network, ever storing your key in a centralized place.
109.ap: The system generates a key pair on your phone (one private, one public). Instead of storing this on a SIM, the public key goes into a cryptographic list called a Merkle Tree—a structure that creates one fingerprint for all authorized keys. The network then checks: does this person produce a zero-knowledge proof that (1) their public key is in that fingerprint's tree and (2) they control the matching private key? The proof is created using special mathematical tricks (Groth16) that are fast to verify but don't leak the key.
109.ww: Zero-knowledge proofs let you prove a fact without revealing the proof. Using a Merkle Tree means no one needs to store your actual key—just a tree fingerprint. And because the proof is mathematically airtight (not dependent on trusting servers), a hacker stealing one proof can't use it twice or forge a new one. The fast verification math (Groth16) makes it practical for millions of authentications.
109.po: Phone networks can now authenticate users without SIM cards and without storing private keys anywhere that can be breached. This eliminates the risk of large-scale SIM data theft while keeping authentication just as fast. Users get better privacy and security without noticing any change.

110.bp: Social networks and biological systems are constantly changing—people join and leave, relationships strengthen or fade. When we detect groups in these networks, we want to know not just 'who is in which cluster' but 'why did this group form and how is it changing?' Black-box algorithms give answers but no explanations, which is dangerous in healthcare (why were these patients grouped together?) or traffic networks (which roads might cause accidents?). We need dynamic clustering that humans can understand.
110.wh: Explaining clustering is hard because the reason someone belongs to a group depends on their role in the network. A hub (connected to many others) belongs differently than a bridge (connecting two groups) or a newcomer (just arrived). Traditional explanations treat all nodes the same. But different roles need different explanations. Also, network clusters change over time, and you have to explain not just 'who is clustered' but 'why did this split happen?'
110.ap: The system learns two separate representations for each person: one captures their role (hub, bridge, connector, etc.—five predefined roles), the other captures which cluster they belong to. These are kept orthogonal (independent) so that a hub in cluster A isn't confused with a hub in cluster B. The system then turns these abstract representations into concrete semantic concepts—prototypes—so an LLM can reason about them. Finally, a hierarchical reasoning process generates explanations at multiple levels: local ('why is this node near its neighbors'), community level ('what's the role pattern in this cluster'), and global ('how did clusters shift').
110.ww: Separating role from cluster membership prevents the system from using one concept to explain the other (a common pitfall). By creating named role prototypes that LLMs understand naturally ('Leader,' 'Wanderer'), you can hand the continuous numbers to an LLM and get human-readable explanations. Hierarchical reasoning covers both static snapshots and temporal changes.
110.po: Doctors, city planners, and social scientists can now see not just the clusters but understand them: 'this community has three leaders and many contributors' or 'this group lost a key connector last week.' The explanations help verify that clustering is sensible and catch errors early.

111.bp: Imagine a group voting on whether to approve a new policy. Each person has private information that hints at what the right choice is, but they don't know the full picture. If they vote their true beliefs, the group might decide correctly. But if they can secretly talk to each other and coordinate, they might vote as a bloc to force a bad outcome. How much secret coordination ability (coalition size) makes this possible, and when can we still trust majority voting?
111.wh: Game theory has two extreme models: either agents vote independently (no coordination), or they can form any secret agreement they want (unlimited coordination). Neither matches reality. In real politics or organizations, small groups (friends, allies) can coordinate, but large conspiracies are hard to keep quiet. The question is: given a specific coalition size that people can secretly coordinate, when does voting still converge to the 'right' answer (informed majority decision)?
111.ap: The researchers define a k-strong equilibrium: a voting outcome where no group of up to k people can deviate to improve their collective outcome (their payoff from the true result they collectively prefer). They then characterize when such equilibria match the informed majority decision (what everyone would choose if the truth were known). The analysis depends on three levers: how big coalitions can be (k), what fraction of people prefer the majority result (information structure), and how concentrated that information is.
111.ww: By making coordination ability explicit and bounded, the model captures the middle ground between chaos and full conspiracy. The characterization reveals that the boundary between 'majority voting works' and 'it fails' is jagged and nonlinear—small changes in k or information distribution can flip the outcome. This matches the intuition that small-group coordination is powerful but fragile.
111.po: Organizations and voting bodies can now reason about: if we assume people can secretly coordinate in groups up to size 10 (or 100), can we still trust majority voting? The answer depends on the specific information structure and shows where voting is robust and where it breaks down, guiding mechanism design.

112.bp: Large language models are trained to generate text, but they often make up facts—hallucinating information that never appeared in their training data. One fix is to give them access to knowledge bases (Wikipedia, Wikidata, etc.) so they can cite real facts. But most methods convert the knowledge base into text, losing the structured relationships that make knowledge bases valuable. We need LLMs to directly use graph-structured knowledge without converting it to messy text.
112.wh: Knowledge graphs (like Wikidata) encode information as relationships: 'Barack Obama' —[born]—> '1961' —[in location]—> 'Hawaii.' If you convert that graph to text, it becomes sequential and loses the structure—the LLM can't easily 'navigate' the graph or see that multiple paths lead to the same fact. Text also bloats the input, wasting the LLM's context window. But LLMs natively understand vectors (lists of numbers), not graph nodes.
112.ap: ConceptFormer learns a mapping from each knowledge graph node (like 'Barack Obama') to a vector representation (a 'concept vector') that the LLM can process natively. Instead of putting the graph into text, you inject these concept vectors directly into the LLM's embedding space—the internal numerical representation where words live. The graph structure is encoded in how the concept vectors relate to each other, without ever being serialized into text.
112.ww: Vectors can preserve graph structure implicitly: nodes that are nearby in the graph end up with similar vectors, and the LLM can use these to infer relationships. By keeping the LLM frozen and only training the concept vector mapping, you avoid retraining a billion-parameter model. And because concept vectors stay in the embedding space where the LLM already operates, the LLM doesn't have to learn a new 'language' to use them.
112.po: LLMs grounded with concept vectors show massive gains in factual recall—up to 272% improvement on Wikipedia sentences. This makes knowledge-grounded LLM systems more trustworthy for question-answering, fact-checking, and any task where accuracy depends on real world knowledge.

113.bp: Graph neural networks (GNNs) make decisions by passing information between connected nodes. When you want to know why the network made a specific decision ('why did you classify this node as fraudulent?'), you need to find which edges and nodes were most important. But real-world graphs are messy—edges get added or deleted by noise or error. An explanation that's fragile to noise is useless because small data errors will break it.
113.wh: GNNs amplify noise through message passing: each node gets information from its neighbors, which got information from their neighbors, and so on. One noisy edge early in this chain can snowball, flipping the output. Existing explanation methods identify important edges but don't account for this amplification. Also, real graphs are heterogeneous: different edge types (friendship, follow, retweet) carry different meanings, and an explanation needs to respect that.
113.ap: RoHeX first analyzes how different GNN architectures amplify noise—revealing which operations are most vulnerable. It then uses a denoising step: a probabilistic model that filters out likely noise and reconstructs a clean graph structure. The explanation is then computed using information bottleneck theory (a mathematical principle that balances how much information you keep versus how much you compress). Edge types are tracked throughout, so the final explanation respects heterogeneity.
113.ww: Understanding how noise amplifies lets you design defenses at the right places in the network. Denoising before explanation makes the explanation robust: it's based on the likely-true graph, not the noisy one. Information bottleneck theory ensures explanations are not just faithful (matching the model's actual decision) but also compact and meaningful—they identify the smallest set of edges that matter most.
113.po: When GNNs are used on messy real data (social networks, recommender graphs, fraud detection), their explanations now remain stable even if the data is noisy. Users and auditors get reliable insight into why the model made a decision, enabling safer deployment in high-stakes domains.

114.bp: Recommendation systems struggle when an item is brand new and has no user interaction history (the 'cold-start' problem). You can't use past behavior to rank it. One workaround is to build semantic descriptions of the item (from title, category, metadata) so the system can match it to similar items that do have history. But how you train those descriptions matters enormously—train them separately and they might not generalize well to new items during recommendation.
114.wh: Standard practice trains semantic IDs (descriptions) first on a separate data, then freezes them and trains the recommendation model. But semantic IDs learned on old data might miss what's important for predicting whether a cold-start item will be liked. It's like memorizing a script for an audition and then using that exact memorized version on stage—you're not adapting to the actual performance.
114.ap: SC2 Rec trains semantic IDs and the recommendation model together, but with a twist: it alternates between two goals. First, it makes the loss landscape sharp (small tweaks to parameters cause big changes in loss) for warm-start items (those with history), which forces precise predictions. Then it makes the loss landscape flatter for cold-start items, which means predictions stay stable even if parameters shift slightly. By enforcing consistency between these two landscapes, the system learns semantic IDs that work well on both old and new items.
114.ww: Sharpness and flatness are opposite concepts—sharp predictions are precise, flat predictions are robust. By flattening the loss landscape for cold-start items, you're essentially saying 'even if the semantic ID isn't perfect, the recommendation should still be reasonable.' Training warm and cold items together means the semantic IDs learn to capture features that help both, not just one.
114.po: Cold-start items now get better recommendations without requiring massive amounts of metadata or interaction data. This matters for new products, artists, and videos where there's little history to learn from. Industrial tests confirm the approach works on real recommender systems.

115.bp: Two people want to swap goods—one has a bicycle, wants a skateboard; the other has a skateboard, wants a bicycle. A simple barter. But what if there are dozens of items and dozens of people, all with different valuations? One person might value a bicycle at $200, another at $50. A centralized exchange (marketplace) needs to find trades that make everyone better off and are fair.
115.wh: The obvious approach—maximize total welfare—is easy. But in the process, some people might lose money while others gain a lot. The person who gets cheated won't participate next time, breaking the market. You need trades where every person gets a non-negative profit (non-negative profit constraint). But proving that such trades exist and computing them efficiently is hard. It's NP-hard, meaning no known efficient algorithm exists for the general problem.
115.ap: The researchers prove the problem is computationally intractable (strongly NP-hard) but then design a randomized polynomial-time algorithm that finds allocations with optimal expected welfare, guarantees every agent a non-negative expected profit, and ensures that with near-certainty, even unlucky agents end up close to breaking even (within the value of two items). The algorithm uses randomization to avoid the worst cases that make deterministic methods slow.
115.ww: Randomization sidesteps the computational bottleneck: instead of trying every possible assignment (exponential), the algorithm makes clever random choices that converge to a good solution. Because each person's valuation is private (they might lie), the paper also studies this from a mechanism-design angle—how to ensure truthful revelation of values while maintaining the welfare guarantees.
115.po: Decentralized marketplaces can now run barter exchanges at scale—peer-to-peer item swaps where the system ensures everyone walks away feeling they got a fair deal. This enables new sharing economies and reduces the need for centralized currency (money) when goods can be directly swapped.

116.bp: Recommendation systems currently optimize for one goal: accuracy (suggesting items you'll like). But real users care about multiple things: they want relevant recommendations, but also variety (not the same type every time), fairness (not just the most popular items), and discovering new things. These goals often conflict: the safest recommendation is something popular, but that kills discovery. We need systems that balance all of them based on what each user prefers.
116.wh: Most systems treat all objectives as equally important or locked in fixed weights. But users differ: some prioritize accuracy, others discovery. Also, objectives pull in opposite directions (accuracy + diversity trade off), and you don't know ahead of time which combination will satisfy a user. Traditional multi-objective optimization requires running experiments with many different weight settings, which is slow.
116.ap: The paper proposes five levels of 'autonomy' for recommendation systems, culminating in personalized multi-objective systems where each user gets unique objective weights. To find each user's preferences efficiently, they use Bayesian optimization: a learning method that tries different objective weights, learns from user feedback which combinations work, and focuses on promising regions. They add orthogonal meta-learning: learning a shared foundation across similar users (so one user's preferences help inform another's), but keeping objectives independent so they don't sabotage each other.
116.ww: Bayesian optimization is designed for expensive-to-evaluate objectives—instead of trying 1000 weight combinations, it intelligently samples 10 that are most likely to reveal user preferences. Orthogonal meta-learning works because users often have similar preference structures (both like accuracy, both want some diversity) even if the weights differ. By exploiting that shared structure, the system learns faster.
116.po: Users now get personalized recommendations that balance their unique priorities without anyone having to manually configure weights. Experimental results show this is more satisfying than one-size-fits-all systems, reducing both echo chambers and user frustration.

117.bp: Running AI models directly in web browsers (instead of on cloud servers) is attractive: lower latency, better privacy, no data sent to servers, no ongoing costs. But now the model code and weights live in an untrusted environment (your browser) where anyone with the page open can inspect the code, download the weights, or modify the model. We need a way to hide the model so that even the person running it can't easily steal or reverse-engineer it.
117.wh: JavaScript-based browser models are transparent: an attacker can pause execution, inspect variables in the debugger, and read out the weights directly. Even if you compress or minify the code, it's still human-readable with modern tools. You need to move the model out of JavaScript into a format that's harder to inspect. WebAssembly (a low-level compiled format) is a candidate, but it's still decompilable.
117.ap: WAMO is an obfuscation framework that converts AI models to WebAssembly and applies transformations at the Wasm layer: scrambling the order of computations, splitting weights across multiple variables, rearranging the instruction graph so the model's logic is harder to follow, and inserting dummy operations. This isn't cryptography (can't stop a determined attacker forever), but it raises the difficulty from 'trivial to reverse' to 'would take days or weeks of specialized effort.'
117.ww: Wasm is lower-level than JavaScript, so patterns like 'this variable is the weight matrix' are less obvious to an attacker. By also obfuscating the computation graph (the sequence of operations), you don't just hide individual numbers—you hide the overall architecture. The dummy operations dilute the signal: an attacker has to distinguish real operations from noise. Together, these raise the cyclomatic complexity (measure of code branching) and 'effort' (lines of code × redundancy) dramatically.
117.po: Models deployed in browsers now have meaningful security against extraction and reverse-engineering, protecting intellectual property and enabling more companies to run models client-side. Performance stays nearly identical, and accuracy doesn't degrade, making this a practical defense.

118.bp: When you search for something, results come back as a ranked list. Large language models can now re-rank that list using their reasoning ability, often improving results. But LLMs have limited context: they can only see the query and maybe 10 documents at a time (the 'sliding window'). To rank 100 documents, you run the LLM 10 times, which is slow and expensive. We need LLMs that can see all documents at once.
118.wh: Longer context windows make this possible but create a new problem: How do you tell the model 'here are 100 documents—rank them all' in a way that the model understands which is document 1, which is document 50, which is document 100? Simple position encoding (just numbering them 1–100) doesn't work because LLMs trained on shorter texts don't generalize to longer positions. Also, with 100 documents, even fast LLMs spend a lot of computation checking if every document is relevant to the query (which most aren't).
118.ap: LongRanker uses a hierarchical positional encoding: first, the model learns where each token (word) sits within its document (intra-document encoding), then it learns which document in the full list (inter-document encoding). This separation helps the model extrapolate to longer sequences. Second, it uses top-k attention: instead of the model looking at all 100 documents, it focuses on the query and only the 10 most important documents (computed on the fly), and ignores the rest.
118.ww: Hierarchical encoding separates the 'local' structure (within a document) from the 'global' structure (document index), which is easier to learn than treating position as a single number. Top-k attention reduces computation from quadratic (check every document) to linear (check the top few), because most documents are irrelevant and checking them wastes compute. The model learns to identify relevant documents cheaply before spending effort on them.
118.po: Ranking systems can now use long-context LLMs to re-rank entire result sets in one pass, reducing API calls by 10× and latency by similar amounts. This makes LLM-based ranking practical for production systems, not just research.

119.bp: Short-video platforms (TikTok, YouTube Shorts, Instagram Reels) are now as popular as traditional social media, but recommender systems for these platforms are poorly understood. They're different from traditional recommendation: users skate through hundreds of videos per day, their interests change rapidly, and feedback is often implicit (did they watch to the end?) and noisy. We need large-scale real data to study how these systems should work.
119.wh: Most public datasets are either small (thousands of videos), synthetic (not representative), or proprietary (locked inside tech companies). This makes it hard to benchmark new recommendation algorithms or understand what features matter most. Real short-video recommendation involves balancing cold-start (new videos have no watch history), rapid interest shifts (trends change minute-to-minute), and diverse feedback types (likes, shares, rewatches, all meaning different things).
119.ap: VK-LSVD is a dataset from the VK platform (a major social network) with 40 billion interactions from 10 million users on 20 million videos over six months. It includes rich metadata: embedded descriptions of video content (semantic features learned by video models), multiple feedback signals (watch time, likes, shares, skips), and contextual data (time of day, user location, device type). The dataset is analyzed for quality and then released publicly.
119.ww: Real-world scale is important: algorithms optimized on tiny datasets often fail at billions of interactions (different patterns emerge). Multiple feedback types matter because 'watch to the end' means something different from 'share immediately'—some signals indicate strong preference, others indicate curiosity or novelty. The six-month timeline captures seasonal trends and interest drift that static datasets miss.
119.po: Researchers can now build and test short-video recommenders without proprietary data, accelerating progress in handling rapid interest shifts and cold-start problems. The dataset's use in the live VK RecSys Challenge 2025 demonstrates its real-world relevance.
